newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's first elected president set to bow out.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's first elected president set to bow out.

text.p: Bulgaria's President Zhelyu Zhelev, barred from seeking a second mandate in Sunday's election, has followed the path of other reformers like Mikhail Gorbachev and Lech Walesa into an early and unwanted retirement.

Zhelev, the first freely elected head of state in Bulgaria's 1,300-year history, had to withdraw from this year's presidential contest after losing Europe's first U.S.-style primary election in June to an unknown lawyer Petar Stoyanov.

On Sunday Zhelev, a fierce opponent of the governing Socialist Party, was expected to cast his vote for Stoyanov, a fellow-liberal who now carries the banner for Bulgaria's reinvigorated anti-communist opposition.

Opinion polls have given Stoyanov a big lead over his Socialist opponent, Culture Minister Ivan Marazov, but for the 61-year-old Zhelev, heading for the political wilderness, even an opposition win will bring little joy.

It is an ignominious end for the former dissident philosopher who, like Poland's Walesa and the ex-Soviet Union's Gorbachev, largely symbolises for the outside world Bulgaria's tortuous transition to democracy and a market economy.

"The Zhelev era is over. The philosopher can return to his books, he can begin to write his memoirs in order to continue the same political battles with the same opponents but by other means," the financial daily Pari said this week.

Zhelev, with his dishevelled white hair, bushy black eyebrows and avuncular grin, brought to his job both a folksy informality and a moral weight born of his pre-1989 struggle against Todor Zhivkov's communist regime.
Zhivkov at one stage forbade Zhelev as an "undesirable" to live in Sofia and banned his controversial book "Fascism", which drew parallels between communist and fascist rule.

Bulgaria's post-communist parliament chose Zhelev as president in 1990 and two years later he won a five-year mandate in a nationwide election. The winner of Sunday's contest formally replaces him in January.
Under Bulgaria's post-communist constitution, the president's powers are largely ceremonial but that has never stopped Zhelev from wading into the political fray.

He has wielded his presidential veto frequently, using the Constitutional Court to help him block what he sees as the current government's attempts to curb media freedom and restrict private ownership of land.
Zhelev is not even on speaking terms with Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, whom he has accused of restoring totalitarian methods of rule.
He has attacked the cabinet on a number of issues ranging from Bulgaria's possible membership of NATO -- which he strongly supports -- to its handling of the economic crisis.
Recently he upset Bulgarians across the political spectrum with his calls for a strong Russian-style presidency to avert economic collapse.
Diplomats in Sofia credit Zhelev with helping to keep the country on a peaceful track over the past six years.
Unlike some of its Balkan neighbours, Bulgaria has avoided bloodshed and boasts a vigorous democratic culture and largely unfettered press despite its grave economic woes.

Bulgarians are more ambiguous about Zhelev's legacy. Some critics say his frequent public attacks on governments he does not agree with have degraded the presidency and harmed Bulgaria's image abroad.

They say he has continued to act like a dissident professor rather than a head of state and his thorny relations even with the opposition parites mean he is unlikely to make a speedy return to active political life.
